newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-Strong pound means wider UK Feb trade gap.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Strong pound means wider UK Feb trade gap.

text.p: The pound's spirited rally over the last seven months has so far not damaged Britain's trade balance, but this could come to an end this week when data are expected to show a widening in February's global trade gap.
The Reuter consensus forecast suggests the trade deficit between Britain and the rest of the world widened to 833 million pounds in February from 641 million in January.

It forecasts the more up-to-date but incomplete data covering trade between Britain and countries outside the European Union in March will also show a worsening trade picture. That deficit is forecast to widen to 616 million pounds from 554 million in February.
The data are due at 0830 GMT on Thursday.
"There are signs that the pound's appreciation is now starting to bite into competitiveness," said Dharshini David, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
"The CBI monthly trends continues to sound alarm bells on export orders and we expect export volumes growth to deteriorate further over the course of the year."
British manufacturers, heavily dependent on export markets, have been complaining for many months that the pound's strength is hurting their business.

This has been reflected in business surveys. The Confederation of British Industry said in its March monthly trends inquiry that demand abroad for British manufactured goods fell to its lowest level since November 1993 because of the strong pound.

Until now, the official trade balances have not suffered. Conversely, the deficits have reaped the benefit of the "J-curve" effect over the last few months which saw the strong pound cut the price of imports faster than Britain's trading partners respond to higher export prices.
As a result, the value of imports will fall before the volume of exports starts to suffer.
Some economists said that effect still has some way to run, especially on trade figures with EU countries.

"The J-curve effects from sterling's rise will predominantly come through on the intra-EU trade figures because sterling's rise has been most marked against these currencies," said Michael Saunders, UK economist at Salomon Brothers.
But even the benefits of J-curve effect cannot mask the worsening underlying trade picture.

"Despite the current froth in the data from the J-curve effect, the underlying position is already deteriorating with import growth starting to outpace export growth," said Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Last month's figures showed export volumes fell 0.5 percent in the three months to January while imports grew by 6.0 percent in the period.
This disparity may increase as consumer demand, already robust, picks up further as tax cuts and windfall payments from building societies hit home.
"Import volume may rise even faster in the months to come as domestic demand gathers pace," said David.
